article_title: Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review
citation: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137
title: Improve ESL pronunciation through a holistic policy approach combining increased government budget, stakeholder negotiation, and accurate policy implementation
description: The review argues that improving ESL pronunciation within the CLT framework requires system-level action beyond the classroom: increased government budget allocations, negotiations among stakeholders, and accurate implementation of policies and practices. It states that "Increasing the budget dedicated to education, particularly for ESL programs, can facilitate the acquisition of modern educational technology, professional development for teachers, and the development of specialized pronunciation curriculum materials." It also calls for collaboration among government bodies, institutions, teachers, parents and the community, and for monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.
requirements: Sufficient financial resources; collaboration among government bodies, educational institutions, teachers, parents and the community; monitoring and evaluation mechanisms
constraints: The review frames this approach for the Bangladeshi ESL context within the CLT framework
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation skills
overall communicative competence in English
examples: The review's discussion proposes language labs equipped with audio-visual aids, teacher engagement by policymakers, parental involvement at home, and collaboration with linguists and ESL experts to design pronunciation programs

article_title: Hoot Reading – MTSS Tier III
citation: Hoot Reading — Evidence Summary. (2025). https://www.hootreading.com
title: Deliver one-to-one tutoring through a purpose-built web application requiring only standard student devices
description: The program's technology model keeps participation barriers low: tutoring is delivered through a web application via an internet browser, so students need only computers or tablets with reliable internet access and headphones. This design allows virtual one-to-one tutoring to run within schools without specialized hardware, with school staff supervising at each location while tutors are provided by the program.
requirements: Computers or tablets with reliable internet access and headphones for each participating student
A web application accessible via an internet browser
target_learners: Elementary students in grades 1–4 in school-district settings
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement through virtual one-to-one instruction
examples: Tutoring sessions take place over video call through the company's proprietary platform

article_title: The Essential Supports for School Improvement
citation: Sebring, P. B., Allensworth, E., Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., & Luppescu, S. (2006). The Essential Supports for School Improvement. Research Report, Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Pursue school improvement holistically across all essential supports rather than through narrow interventions
description: Because strength in multiple essential supports is what produces improvement, the report argues that narrow, single-focus interventions will have limited success. It states that "narrow interventions will have limited success in improving student learning," giving the example that technology investments will have little effect if students do not feel safe and classrooms are frequently disrupted. The framework therefore embraces a holistic, coherent view of school development in which all five supports are strengthened together and focused on ambitious instruction.
requirements: Attention to all five essential supports, since a weakness in any organizational element can undermine strengths in other areas
constraints: Derived from Chicago elementary school evidence, 1990-1996; the report notes schools with high concentrations of students with extraordinary needs had few resources remaining to sustain improvement efforts
target_learners: Elementary school students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: Raising student academic achievement through coordinated school development
examples: The report cites investments in integrating technology into the curriculum as having little effect when students do not feel safe and classrooms face frequent disruptions

article_title: Computational Thinking for a Computational World
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Code.org's Hour of Code as the ignition point of the modern coding movement
description: The paper describes Hour of Code, introduced in 2013 by the nonprofit Code.org, as "a one-hour introduction to computer science for K-12 students" that ignited the modern coding movement. With effective marketing, a simple point of access, and a workforce-development narrative, it engaged computer science educators, education leaders, teachers, nonprofits, policymakers, and employers. The paper situates it in a lineage from Papert's Logo and constructionism to Scratch, and notes Code.org's mission emphasizes expanding access and participation by women and underrepresented minorities.
requirements: Simple points of access and broad stakeholder coalitions to sustain movement momentum
constraints: The paper notes the movement's workforce focus troubled some educators who saw education's purpose as broader than job preparation
target_learning_goals: introductory computer science
coding
examples: The paper credits Hour of Code with triggering a social movement after decades of work by ACM, CSTA, ISTE, and NSF had not gained similar popular support

title: How People Learn framework as the pedagogical foundation of the A4L Lessons curriculum

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Conduct a holistic districtwide analysis of existing services and unmet needs to target community schools funding and implementation
description: The principle holds that districts scaling community schools should first analyze what services already exist and what is still needed, using multiple data sources, so that new funds fill genuine gaps rather than duplicating provision. Lynwood leadership used "a combination of referral data tied to the district's health collaborative, climate surveys, and administrative data to pinpoint high areas of need" and gaps in resources, staffing, and partnerships. This analysis drove use of CCSPP funds, such as hiring student support analysts after referral analysis revealed a Tier 3 behavioral support gap.
requirements: Existing service and partnership infrastructure whose use can be traced through data such as referral records, climate surveys, and administrative data
constraints: The report presents this as a lesson from one rapidly scaling district implementing without a prior planning grant; effectiveness evidence is descriptive
target_learners: K-12 students in a high-need, majority low-income district
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, attendance, and access to integrated academic and non-academic supports
examples: Lynwood analyzed health collaborative referrals, climate surveys, and administrative data, then used CCSPP funds to hire four certified student support analysts to address a gap in Tier 3 behavioral supports for general education students without IEPs.

article_title: Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education
citation: Brian Harrington, Irina Zlotnikova, Gayathri Nadarajan, and Samuel Ekundayo. (2025). Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. 26, 1, Article 15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776558
title: Hofstede's cultural dimensions framework as a lens for interpreting cross-cultural differences in GenAI ethical judgments
description: The article uses Hofstede's cultural dimensions theory—power distance, individualism versus collectivism, competitiveness, and uncertainty avoidance—as the theoretical basis for interpreting why Canadian and Korean students judged identical GenAI scenarios differently. Canada is characterized by "low power distance and high individualism," fostering strict anti-plagiarism norms, while Korea's higher power distance and collectivist orientation frame knowledge as communal. The authors argue this model provides "the most precise and contextually appropriate theoretical foundation" for analyzing students' ethical evaluations of GenAI in structured university settings, over alternatives such as Schwartz's values theory or the GLOBE study.
requirements: Application to educational settings requires distinguishing dimensions relevant to authority, rule-following, and uncertainty around emerging technologies
constraints: The authors caution against overgeneralizing cultural patterns, noting misconduct often arises from inadequate institutional support, insufficient training, and language barriers rather than inherent cultural values
target_learning_goals: ethical reasoning about GenAI use in coursework
academic integrity understanding
examples: The study interpreted Canadian students' heightened sensitivity to integrity breaches and Korean students' more permissive attitudes through the low-power-distance/individualist versus high-power-distance/collectivist contrast

article_title: Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing
citation: Lindsay Dawson, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12523
title: Horizontal and vertical transfer framework for guiding AI-assisted problem posing
description: The study employs a conceptual framework, adapted from the authors' prior work on transfer of learning and Jonassen's problem-solving framework, in which problem posing proceeds by "horizontal transfer, where the reader takes explicit information from the problem and tries to align it with pre-created knowledge structures, and vertical transfer, where a reader actively recognizes features of a situation, activating and applying prior knowledge". Horizontal transfer changes a problem's representation or context while keeping the approach the same; vertical transfer alters complexity and requires applying concepts more deeply. The framework was taught in the training video to give students a theoretically grounded basis for posing problems with Gen AI as a guide.
requirements: Students receive training that introduces the framework and prompt-engineering techniques before posing problems
constraints: In prior studies students were not trained with a conceptual framework for posing new problems; this study adapts one to fill that gap
target_learners: prospective engineering majors in first-semester calculus-based physics
target_learning_goals: transfer of learning in physics problem solving
problem-posing skills
examples: The 15-minute training video introduced the conceptual framework along with examples of utilizing prompt engineering to pose a physics problem

article_title: Does Generative Artificial Intelligence Improve Students' Higher-Order Thinking? A Meta-Analysis Based on 29 Experiments and Quasi-Experiments
citation: Zhao Yan, Yue Yuhe, Sun Zhonghua, Jiang Qiang, Li Gangsheng. (2025). Does Generative Artificial Intelligence Improve Students’ Higher-Order Thinking? A Meta-Analysis Based on 29 Experiments and Quasi-Experiments. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13120160
title: Higher-order thinking as an integrated three-component capacity: critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving ability
description: The article adopts a conceptualization of higher-order thinking rooted in Bloom's taxonomy and its revision, in which HOT is "an integrated cognitive capacity, highly dependent on metacognitive awareness". Its core components are held to be critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving ability, which the authors describe as activated synergistically in complex problem situations: critical thinking analyzes and evaluates information, creative thinking generates diverse solutions, and problem-solving ability constructs and implements strategies. The meta-analysis operationalizes HOT through these three dimensions.
requirements: Outcome measures must be classifiable into critical thinking, creativity, or problem-solving dimensions for the meta-analytic synthesis to apply
constraints: The article notes that specific classifications of HOT vary across disciplinary contexts, with discipline-specific dimensional lists differing from the cross-disciplinary consensus
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
creative thinking
problem-solving ability
examples: Table 1 summarizes disciplinary classifications, e.g., mathematics education listing critical thinking, creative thinking, problem-solving skills, and metacognition

article_title: Transforming clicks into critical thinking: An AI-based media literacy program for children
citation: Demir, R., & Akar, C. (2025). Transforming Clicks into Critical Thinking: An AI-Based Media Literacy Program for Children. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6786882/v1
title: Hobbs's five-part media literacy model operationalized through participatory culture theory
description: The study's theoretical foundation combines Hobbs's five-domain media literacy framework with Jenkins's participatory culture theory. The article states: "The theoretical foundation of this study draws from Hobbs's (2011) ve-part media literacy model—access, analysis, evaluation, creation, and re ection—stressing learner agency in meaning-making and content creation." This model is operationalized through Jenkins's (2009) Participatory Culture Theory, which sees learners as active contributors in digital spaces rather than mere consumers. In the discussion, the authors report that students demonstrated gains across all five dimensions and that the integration proved "pedagogically coherent and practically viable."
requirements: Instruction that engages learners as active contributors and creators of media content, not only consumers
constraints: The framework was implemented and evaluated in a single fourth-grade setting in Turkey; the authors note the sample size and geographic scope may limit generalizability
target_learning_goals: critical analysis, evaluation, and creation of media
learner agency in meaning-making
participatory digital citizenship
examples: ChatGPT and Perplexity AI supported source interrogation and balanced reasoning, while Canva AI and Grammarly supported students in generating their own ethical and creative media outputs, mapped onto the five domains.

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: Integrate AI into STEM education by considering the whole educational system, not merely applying AI technologies
description: The review's guiding principle is that high-quality STEM education with AI requires holistic integration rather than technology deployment alone. As the article states, achieving a high quality of STEM education requires careful consideration of complex social, pedagogical, environmental factors rather than merely applying AI technologies. Grounded in general system theory, applying AI as an external technology element influences the other system elements (subject, information, medium, environment) and the relationships between them, so selection of AI techniques should adapt to these multiple elements.
requirements: AI technique selection must adapt to the multiple elements (e.g., subject, information, environment) in STEM education with the goal of high-quality instruction and learning
constraints: The article notes the field is confronted with the challenge of integrating diverse AI techniques in the complex STEM educational system
target_learners: STEM learners and instructors across educational levels
target_learning_goals: High-quality STEM instruction and learning supported by AI technologies
examples: The review mapped how each AI category distributed across learning contents, instructional strategies, educational levels, media, and contexts to inform integration decisions

article_title: Executive Functions in Children Who Experience Bullying Situations
citation: Medeiros W, Torro-Alves N, Malloy-Diniz LF and Minervino CM (2016) Executive Functions in Children Who Experience Bullying Situations. Front. Psychol. 7:1197. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01197
title: Hot and cold executive functions dichotomy applied to bullying roles
description: The article organizes its findings using the Kerr and Zelazo (2004) distinction between executive function types: "hot (more closely related to motivation and emotional control) and cold (more closely related to logical-rational aspects of cognition) executive functions." Cold functions cover inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility following Diamond's three-core model, while hot functions cover affective decision-making assessed with the Iowa Gambling Task. The authors use this dichotomy to interpret their pattern of results: victims showed greater difficulty on cold tasks whereas bullies showed impairment on the hot task.
requirements: Assessment must separately measure hot components (affective decision-making) and cold components (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility) to distinguish role profiles.
constraints: The article states its methodology was transversal, so causal inferences about the investigated aspects cannot be made.
target_learning_goals: executive functioning and affective decision-making in social behavior regulation
examples: Bullies were impaired on the hot executive function task (IGT Deck A choices) while victims performed worse on cold tasks (TMT-B), supporting the dichotomy's application to bullying roles.

article_title: Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes
citation: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311
title: Hot/cool distinction in executive function: cool EF as logic-driven and hot EF as emotion-driven processes underlying goal-directed behavior
description: Executive function is an umbrella term for skills essential for conscious, goal-directed thought and behavior. The framework separates cool EF — psychological processes involving pure logic and critical analysis, elicited under abstract, decontextualized, non-affective conditions (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, attentional control, planning) — from hot EF, which "involves goal-directed, future-oriented cognitive processes elicited in contexts that generate emotion, motivation, and a tension between instant gratiﬁcation and long-term rewards," including delay gratification and affective decision making. The study uses this distinction to test differential adolescent development and outcome contributions.
requirements: Measurement batteries must separately capture affectively loaded decision contexts (e.g., gambling tasks) and abstract non-affective tasks to operationalize the two facets
constraints: The article notes current research does not make a convincing case for the distinction of the hot and cool forms, though EF is generally agreed to specialize into distinct functions with development
target_learning_goals: goal-directed behavior and self-regulation underlying academic performance and psychological adjustment
examples: The study operationalized cool EF with backward digit span, CNT, Stockings of Cambridge, and Stroop, and hot EF with the Cambridge Gambling Task's risk adjustment and delay aversion measures
key_sources: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311

article_title: Cultural differences in online learning: International student perceptions
citation: Liu, X., Liu, S., Lee, S.-h., & Magjuka, R. J. (2010). Cultural Differences in Online Learning: International Student Perceptions. Educational Technology & Society, 13(3), 177-188. https://www.jstor.org/stable/jeductechsoci.13.3
title: Hofstede's four-dimensional model of cultural differences as a framework for interpreting cross-cultural online learning
description: Hofstede's model characterizes cultural behaviors along four dimensions: power distance, individualism-collectivism, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity-femininity. The article states that "Hofstede developed a four-dimensional model of cultural differences, which can be used to characterize cultural behaviors that originate from different societies." The authors used this framework to interpret their interview findings, linking students' collectivism, high power distance and uncertainty avoidance to their preferences for structured instruction, group work and reliance on instructors and textbooks. The article notes the model has been criticized as essentialist but considers it a valid framework for analyzing cultural differences in teaching and learning.
requirements: The framework is used to interpret findings about culturally different pedagogical objectives and expectations between teachers and students from different societies
constraints: The article notes the model has been challenged on external validity and labeled an essentialist model of culture emphasizing fixity of identity
target_learners: international students in transnational online programs
target_learning_goals: understanding cultural differences affecting participation and design of online courses
examples: The authors interpreted Eastern students' modest, face-saving personalities and preference for group work as reflecting collectivism and femininity, and U.S. students' independence and competitiveness as individualism and masculinity

article_title: Life Stress Impairs Self-Control in Early Adolescence
citation: Duckworth, A. L., Kim, B., and Tsukayama, E. (2013). Life stress impairs self-control in early adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00608
title: Hot/cool dual-process account: stress shifts processing toward the hot, impulsive system
description: The article interprets its findings through the hot/cool model (Metcalfe and Mischel, 1999), which "contrasts two opponent systems": a cool system that is "affectively-neutral, flexible, slow, and strategic" and a hot system that is "impulsive and reflexive, responding quickly to salient trigger features." Perceived stress is postulated to modulate the balance, so that as stress increases the cool system becomes dysfunctional and the hot system dominates. The authors present their longitudinal findings as direct, real-world evidence consistent with this account, which previously rested on animal and laboratory studies.
requirements: The account presupposes that perceived stress modulates the relative activity of the two systems
constraints: The article offers this as indirect interpretive support, not a direct test of the model
target_learning_goals: self-control over attentional, behavioral, and emotional impulses
examples: The three longitudinal studies are presented as direct evidence that children are more impulsive when negotiating stressful life circumstances

article_title: How the home learning environment contributes to children’s social–emotional competence: A moderated mediation model
citation: Li S, Tang Y and Zheng Y (2023) How the home learning environment contributes to children's social–emotional competence: A moderated mediation model. Front. Psychol. 14:1065978. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1065978
title: Three-dimension conceptualization of the home learning environment grounded in the bio-ecological model
description: The article conceptualizes the home learning environment within the bio-ecological model of human development, distinguishing distal and proximal processes. It defines three dimensions: "structural family characteristics, parental beliefs and interests, and educational processes", with educational processes at the core as the proximal "engine" of development. Distal factors include family income, occupational status, and parental educational beliefs; proximal processes are parent–child interactions in educational activities such as reading, singing, and play. The framework underpins the study's hypothesized moderated mediation model.
requirements: The framework assumes parents and teachers can report reliably on home learning environment and child competence via questionnaires
constraints: Conceptualized for children aged 3–6 in the Chinese preschool context
The article notes no general or common operational definition of home learning environment exists across studies
target_learning_goals: social–emotional competence development including cognitive control, emotional expressivity, empathy and prosocial behaviors, and emotion regulation
examples: The study operationalized the three dimensions in a revised Home Learning Environment Questionnaire with 30 items and tested them in a latent variable SEM with 443 children

title: A taxonomy classifying authentic CSCL learning environments into simulation and hybrid environments with five descriptors

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Develop group awareness tools from a holistic perspective combining cognitive and behavioral information
description: The article concludes that designing GA tools requires a holistic perspective combining both GA information types rather than relying on a single type alone. Because cognitive and behavioral challenges co-occur in wiki learning, and the article argues the two GA information types complement each other, tool developers should present both knowledge-level and participation-level information together in wiki environments.
requirements: Both the cognitive challenge of selecting meaningful content and the behavioral challenge of stimulating active contributions must be addressed simultaneously for GA tools to support wiki learning processes fully.
constraints: Providing one type of GA information might not have been enough to make learners aware of how much and what kind of content is desirable.
target_learners: Collaborative writing groups in higher education
target_learning_goals: Improving wiki article quality
Supporting collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The study's combination condition presented knowledge bars and participation bars simultaneously in a wiki discussion forum on energy sources, alongside single-type and control conditions for comparison.

article_title: Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior
citation: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3
title: Homework management as a five-dimension volitional self-regulation framework
description: The article frames homework management as students' use of self-regulated learning strategies during homework, grounded in volitional control — the ability to stay oriented toward goals set by another source, here the teacher. Drawing on Xu and Corno, it treats homework management as five dimensions: "environmental structuring, time management, distraction management, motivation monitoring, and emotion management", operationalized in the Homework Management Scale. In this study the framework is modeled as a latent mediator between teacher homework involvement and homework behavior in Turkish secondary students.
requirements: Students must be motivated to use the strategies; the article states students use self-regulation skills when they want to, so factors increasing motivation increase strategy use
constraints: The article notes self-regulation skill use varies by school level: acquired but little used in primary school, frequently used in secondary school, and not preferred in high school
target_learning_goals: completing homework independently
applying self-regulation strategies such as time management and emotion control during homework
examples: The study measured the five dimensions with the 22-item Turkish-adapted Homework Management Scale and modeled them as indicators of a latent homework management variable

Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Schraw et al.'s four-component framework of higher-order thinking, with CT as a subcomponent
description: The review presents HOT as an overarching concept of "skills that enhance the construction of deeper, conceptually-driven understanding," aligned with Bloom's taxonomy levels above remembering. It reports that "HOT has been put forward as having four components (Schraw et al., 2011): (a) reasoning (i.e., induction and deduction), (b) argumentation (i.e., generating and evaluating evidence and arguments), (c) metacognition (i.e., thinking about and regulating one's thinking), and (d) problem solving and critical thinking (CT)." In this framework CT is treated as a subcomponent of HOT, and alternative characterizations add creative thinking as a possible further component.
requirements: Knowledge remains essential: the framework holds that knowledge is needed and related to thinking processes
constraints: The review acknowledges its definitions are selective, focusing on those relevant to student-centered learning environments rather than all philosophical, psychological, and educational traditions
target_learning_goals: Reasoning, argumentation, metacognition, problem solving, and critical thinking
examples: The two included HOT studies (Sasson et al., 2018; Sugeng & Suryani, 2020) operationalized HOT via Bloom's taxonomy levels of application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation

title: Hoover-Dempsey model of the parental involvement process
description: The article describes the Hoover-Dempsey model as explaining "the antecedents of parental involvement, consequences on child adjustments, and mediation pathways". It highlights three key family-level antecedents: parental motivational beliefs (active role construction and "a strong sense of self-efficacy that they can make positive impacts on children's learning"), perceptions of whether school, teacher, or child want involvement, and contextual family factors. The meta-analysis findings support the model's placement of parenting self-efficacy as a key antecedent of parents' contributions to the home-school partnership.

constraints: The article notes only the self-efficacy component of motivational beliefs was considered in its inclusion criteria

examples: The meta-analysis tested the model's prediction that parenting self-efficacy is a key antecedent of parents' partnership contributions

article_title: Does Spelling Still Matter—and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research
citation: Steven C. Pan, Timothy C. Rickard, Robert A. Bjork. (2021). Does Spelling Still Matter— and If So, How Should It Be Taught? Perspectives from Contemporary and Historical Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09611-y
title: Horn-Ashbaugh Speller weekly curriculum: distributed practice and retrieval practice with pretesting, self-testing, and spaced review
description: The Speller's curriculum assigned a new word list each Monday with a pretest, self-testing study routines on Tuesday and Thursday (look, visualize, cover, write from memory, check, repeated three times), diagnostic tests on Wednesday and Friday that also assessed the list from one month prior, and a spelling notebook tracking errors and progress. The review characterizes these as implementations of "distributed practice" and "practice testing" (retrieval practice), two techniques "now regarded as evidence-based and highly robust". The pattern also included reviewing difficult words at the start of each school year.
requirements: Requires daily instructional time devoted to spelling, weekly word lists, and teacher-administered pretests and diagnostic tests with corrective feedback
constraints: The review judges the Speller overall obsolete: its visualization-heavy drill routines rested on an incomplete view of spelling's cognitive mechanisms, and it lacked grade-level benchmarks and systematic error diagnosis
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of assigned word lists
development of a spelling conscience and motivation to spell correctly
examples: The Speller contained grade-appropriate lists totaling 4578 words and prescribed a daily routine of testing, writing, and word study exercises, remaining a bestseller for at least 25 years

article_title: Maternal homework assistance and children's task-persistent behavior in elementary school
citation: Viljaranta, J., Silinskas, G., Lerkkanen, M.-K., Hirvonen, R., Pakarinen, E., Poikkeus, A.-M., & Nurmi, J.-E. (2017). Maternal Homework Assistance and Children’s Task-Persistent Behavior in Elementary School. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Maternal+Homework+Assistance+and+Children%E2%80%99s+Task-Persistent+Behavior+in+Elementary+School
title: Self-determination theory-based typology of maternal homework assistance: help, monitoring, and autonomy granting
description: The article applies self-determination theory to distinguish three types of maternal homework assistance by their level of direct involvement. Autonomy granting means trusting the child to work independently; help is active, direct involvement — "in terms of the parent actively and directly helping the child with homework tasks by, for example, sitting next to the child and working on the task together"; monitoring is lower-involvement checking that homework is complete and correct. Help and monitoring are seen as more controlling practices that may diminish children's feelings of autonomy and competence, whereas autonomy granting satisfies needs for autonomy and competence and supports motivated, persistent behavior.
requirements: Distinguishing the three types requires measuring the amount of each practice separately, as different types are differently related to children's outcomes
constraints: The article measures the amount (frequency) of assistance via mothers' self-reports, not its quality, and treats help and monitoring as general rather than subject-specific constructs
target_learning_goals: task-persistent behavior in learning situations
academic performance in math and reading
examples: Mothers rated the frequency of help, monitoring, and autonomy granting on identical 10-item questionnaires in Grades 2, 3, and 4, with three factors extracted at all time points

article_title: Exploring the short-term and long-term effects of the COVID-19 school closures on reading fluency in Southern Germany: A longitudinal causal effects analysis
citation: Kraus, E. B., Wild, J., Schilcher, A., & Hilbert, S. (2024). Exploring the Short-Term and Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 School Closures on Reading Fluency in Southern Germany: A Longitudinal Causal Effects Analysis. https://osf.io/bu2ad/
title: Control time-dependent trends in causal learning-loss analyses by choosing a homogeneously developing, narrowly defined ability measured with a standardized instrument
description: This design principle holds that causal estimates of instructional disruptions require tight confinement of the counterfactual trend. The authors achieved this by restricting the outcome to reading fluency, "a readily measurable and well-defined construct", and by noting that "the choice of an ability with a homogeneous development, a narrow definition of the construct reading fluency, and the measurement with a standardized instrument allowed us to control time-dependent trends in our causal analysis." Multiple measurement points additionally separated short-term from long-term effects.
requirements: A standardized, normed test instrument usable across the full study period
Large sample sizes and high data quality for pre-trend and matched control comparison
Pre-trend estimation and propensity score weighting to validate the parallel assumption
constraints: Findings apply to a skill assumed mostly internalized and automated before the disruption; skills still developing, such as third-grade reading comprehension, may show more severe impact
Sample restricted to one region (Bavaria) and one grade, limiting generalization
target_learners: elementary school students (grades two to four)
target_learning_goals: reading fluency
examples: The study restricted the sample to Southern German third graders, used the SLS across five measurement points, and validated linear pre-trends before estimating DiD effects.

article_title: Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills
citation: Torppa, M., Psyridou, M., Khanolainen, D., Koponen, T., & Salminen, J. (2025). Role of home math environment in the intergenerational transmission of math skills. Learning and Instruction, 97, Article 102080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102080
title: Home Numeracy Model: formal vs. informal home math activities as distinct categories
description: The Home Numeracy Model (Skwarchuk et al., 2014), adopted in this study, divides math-related parent–child interactions into two categories. Formal activities are instructional, with the "purposeful aim of parents teaching math content to their children," such as counting objects or printing numbers. Informal activities are playful or real-world tasks in which math content is incidentally present, such as playing board games or measuring ingredients while cooking. The study adopted this categorization because it was empirically well fitted to the data structure and enables comparison with previous research.
requirements: Parental self-report questionnaires on frequency of shared math-related activities, rated on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all or rarely) to 5 (several times a day)
constraints: The authors acknowledge that assessment of HME is very intricate and this categorization is a simplified representation of the complex nature of HME
target_learning_goals: Early arithmetic fluency development
examples: In this study, factor analyses identified one formal and one informal HME factor at age 2, and three factors (formal, games, everyday activities) at age 5 and Grade 1

article_title: Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher–student relationships and student learning.
citation: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/
title: In field settings, design relationship interventions holistically so teachers can flexibly use strategies from their existing repertoire
description: The article argues that in noisy, complex field settings, interventions targeting narrowly defined constructs risk having their effects drowned out, and that precisely specified interventions may be dropped once a study ends. Instead, it recommends that "an intervention that engages teachers in using strategies from their existing repertoire that they can flexibly incorporate into their daily practices, would seem to have a greater chance of adoption over the long term." The study's own induction followed this logic by scaffolding multiple pathways rather than prescribing one strategy.
requirements: Interventions must offer teachers sufficient latitude to execute the approach in ways that work for them
Constructs should be conceptualized broadly enough that discrete-component improvements can propagate to broader outcomes
constraints: The article presents this as a design rationale for field experiments, not as a directly tested manipulation
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher-student relationships and downstream student outcomes
examples: The induction encouraged use of different strategies, provided colleague feedback, and asked teachers to propose their own action steps rather than prescribing a single perspective taking routine

article_title: Comparative tests of home work and school work.
citation: Heck, W. H. (1914). Comparative tests of home work and school work. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412814
title: Do not assign home work that requires equipment, literature, or assistance many homes cannot furnish
description: The article draws an equity boundary for home work assignments: tasks "requiring equipment, literature, assistance, etc., which many homes of the students concerned cannot furnish, are manifestly unjust and should not be given in public schools." Sensible assignments instead call for independent work on topics previously discussed in school, for which the majority of homes are about as favorable as the majority of schools.
requirements: Home work topics should have been previously discussed in school so no outside resources are needed
constraints: Assignments depending on equipment, literature, or assistance unavailable in many homes are unjust in public schools
target_learners: public school students in grammar and high school grades
target_learning_goals: independent practice of school-taught content
examples: The composition topics ('The Harrisonburg High School', 'The Town of Harrisonburg') were chosen so any high school student had enough facts in mind, with no need to consult outsiders or literature.

article_title: Comparative tests of home work and school work.
citation: Heck, W. H. (1914). Comparative tests of home work and school work. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412814
title: Home work and school work are about equal and both depend on good teaching
description: The article's final conclusion from experiments in arithmetic and English composition, chosen to represent two contrasted types of school requirements, is that "home work and school work are or can be made about equal to each other, are about equally dependent on good teaching, and will therefore develop as the teaching develops." Objections to home work on grounds of supposed inferiority are not justified; the two should not be pitted against each other but improved together through clear instruction, assignment, interest, and checking of results.
requirements: Good teaching in school and home co-operation, including clear instruction and assignment, creation of interest, and strict checking-up of results
constraints: As a matter of daily routine children may not know how or may not will to do either well without good teaching
target_learning_goals: arithmetic computation and reasoning
English composition
examples: The Harrisonburg experiments assigned matched test forms to balanced groups so each group did one computation and one reasoning test, or one composition, in each environment.

article_title: An update on recent advances in targeted memory reactivation during sleep
citation: Julia Carbone & Susanne Diekelmann. (2024). An update on recent advances in targeted memory reactivation during sleep. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00244-8
title: Home-use TMR and dream-incubation devices (Dreem headband, Dormio, SleepStim, Ezzence)
description: The review describes a set of devices enabling TMR outside the lab: the Dreem headband delivers sounds via bone-conduction transducers during REM sleep; 'Dormio' is a wearable for targeted dream incubation during the hypnagogic period; 'SleepStim' pairs a smartwatch and smartphone with "a machine-learning model ... to identify periods of deep sleep to trigger TMR sounds"; and 'Ezzence' is a smartphone-controlled olfactometer releasing odors during specific sleep stages.
requirements: Devices must either detect target sleep stages (e.g., via EEG or movement/heart-rate machine-learning classification) or be used in procedures tolerant of unmonitored sleep.
constraints: SleepStim experiments found the memory benefit depended on sound intensity and sleep stage, with greater improvements at lower intensity and when cues were delivered in SWS; Ezzence feasibility was tested without yet validating it for TMR.

procedural skill memory
dream content shaping
examples: social-anxiety patients used the Dreem headband for a week of REM cueing at home
a pilot found 67% of Dormio awakenings incorporated the cued word 'tree'
SleepStim was tested over three subsequent nights of object-location cueing

article_title: Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures
citation: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8
title: Hofstede's cultural dimensions as a post-hoc framework for interpreting cross-cultural help-seeking differences
description: The article applies Hofstede's cultural dimensions—Masculinity, Individualism, and Power Distance—to interpret why effective help seeking diverged across sites. It suggests Philippine and U.S. students may have "viewed work on the ITS as a competition" consistent with their higher Masculinity scores, while lower Power Distance may have let Costa Rican students informally collaborate despite instructions to work individually. The authors emphasize these are post-hoc speculations not directly tested.
requirements: Empirical research across a larger number of sites is stated as necessary to determine whether these dimensions best explain the results
constraints: The article states it did not test the relationship between Hofstede's dimensions and student behaviors directly; Philippines respondents scored similarly to Costa Rica on Individualism yet behaved differently, so that dimension alone could not explain the results
target_learners: Students aged 12-14 using intelligent tutoring systems in Costa Rica, the Philippines, and the United States
target_learning_goals: Help seeking as a cross-curricular self-regulation skill in mathematics learning
examples: The article links Hofstede survey scores for the three countries to observed classroom behaviors, e.g., Philippine students heeding teacher directions and working silently and alone

description: Fresh Start groups pupils for small-group teaching according to scores on its own screening assessment, so that each group is homogeneous in reading ability. title: Holt-Laury public goods card game run with clickers as a classroom experiment
description: A classroom experiment illustrating public goods as a special case of market failure, using the game "designed by Holt and Laury (1997)" to illustrate "the concepts of non-rivalry and non-excludabil- ity" and the free-rider market failure. Students receive two black and two red cards; playing a red card is a contribution to the public good worth a dollar to all, while keeping red cards earns four dollars privately. The authors modified the game with clickers so students chose among three contribution options privately, reducing dead time between rounds and freeing time for class discussion conducted only after all rounds.
requirements: Multiple rounds with the value of a red card changed across rounds, followed by whole-class discussion relating experiment outcomes to the concept of public goods
constraints: In the study it was used as a single experiment inside a traditional lecture-based course, where it did not translate into significant overall learning gains
target_learning_goals: understanding public goods, non-rivalry, non-excludability, the free-rider problem and market failure as a rationale for government intervention
examples: Three macro sections (84 students) played the clicker-modified card game while a micro control section (28 students) received traditional lecture on the same content

citation: Marine Houssa, Nathalie Nader-Grosbois. (2016). Experimental Study of Middle-term Training in Social Cognition in Preschoolers. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i1.972
title: Combined ToM and SIP training program with hierarchical progression for preschoolers
description: The article describes a 15-session middle-term training combining Theory of Mind and social information processing, built on "a hierarchical progression (from simple to complex abilities)": seven ToM sessions, seven SIP sessions, and a final integration session. It draws on Howlin et al.'s mental-state progression, the six steps of the Crick and Dodge SIP model, and Barisnikov et al.'s justification levels, eliciting more complex justifications via the zone of proximal development. Sessions used varied materials, open-ended questions, and differentiated immediate feedback.
requirements: Sessions are administered in small groups of about 4 children by trained experimenters, with varied materials and differentiated immediate feedback
constraints: The article notes trained children used hardly any conceptual-level justification, which generally emerges later in development
target_learners: typically developing preschoolers aged 4 to 5 years 4 months
target_learning_goals: Theory of Mind competences (emotions and beliefs)
social information processing and social problem solving
examples: Sessions used sequences of play, pictures, video extracts, handling of objects, puppets and story reading, each ending with a story dealing with an emotion, a false belief or a social problem solving situation

article_title: Changing Perceptions of Teachers Regarding the Importance and Competence of Their Principals as Leaders
citation: Grobler, B., Bisschoff, T., & Beeka, A. (2012). Changing perceptions of teachers regarding the importance and competence of their principals as leaders. South African Journal of Education, 32(1), 40-55. https://journals.co.za/handle/10520/EJC132899
title: Leadership development programmes for school principals should be grounded in a holistic model addressing multiple interdependent dimensions.
description: The article demonstrates that a structured intervention programme based on the seven dimensions of holistic leadership can positively change teachers' perceptions of their principals' competence. The programme used "multiple modes of presentation such as group work and self-reflection strategies" and engaged principals in debating, naming, and exploring causal links among the seven factors. This suggests that leadership development should address the interdependent dimensions holistically rather than in isolation.
requirements: Intervention programmes must engage principals actively with the interconnections among leadership dimensions, not merely present them as separate topics.
constraints: The intervention lasted only one day with one follow-up workshop, and the article notes the short period between training and data gathering as a limitation.
target_learning_goals: Develop competence across multiple leadership dimensions
Shift from bureaucratic to collaborative leadership practices
examples: Twenty principals completed questionnaires, debated factor names, proposed causal links among the seven factors, and compared their models to the confirmed Beeka (2009) model.

article_title: With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving
citation: Frederick, M. L., Courtney, S., & Caniglia, J. (2014). With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Holton and Clarke's scaffolding domains and metacognition account
description: The article presents Holton and Clarke's (2006) account in which scaffolding is "an act of teaching that (a) supports the immediate construction of knowledge by the learner; and (b) provides the basis for the future independent learning of the individual". It broadens scaffolding into four main elements, of which conceptual scaffolding (promoting conceptual development) and heuristic scaffolding (developing problem-solving heuristics that transcend specific content) constitute the domains. The account links scaffolding to metacognition and to Vygotsky's zone of proximal development.
requirements: Scaffolding must support immediate knowledge construction and future independent learning, not merely provide facts or direct demonstration
constraints: Not everything used in the classroom actually assists learning and teaching; simply providing facts or directly showing students how to do something would not be considered scaffolding
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem solving
metacognition
self-scaffolding
examples: The study used the heuristic and conceptual scaffolding domains as part of its underlying framework for employing grouping and graphic-organizer scaffolds concurrently

description: The HA is the dominant approach to teacher professional development, focused on "encouraging reflection on teaching practices, experiences, and beliefs". In this study HA teachers identified a problem they considered important, formulated action plans, and revised them at monthly group sessions, writing narratives of critical classroom incidents. Unlike the DIA, its reflection was not focused on stage-specific teaching skills drawn from EER, and no HA teacher moved developmental stage.

constraints: The article states the holistic approach does not take into account research evidence that teacher factors can be grouped into developmental stages

examples: HA teachers reflected on successes and failures in teaching and wrote detailed accounts of one critical incident, describing situation, people, feelings and reasoning

Reliable Wi-Fi connectivity

three-dimensional spatial orientation
clinically oriented anatomical reasoning

citation: Schelfhout Stijn, Wille Bart, Fonteyne Lot, Roels Elisabeth, De Fruyt Filip, Duyck Wouter. (2019). The effects of vocational interest on study results: Student person – environment fit and program interest diversity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214618
title: Holland RIASEC hexagon model of vocational interest with homogeneity-based environment profiles
description: The RIASEC theory represents persons (students) and environments (study programs) on "the same clockwise hexagon, containing six dimensions or scales": Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, and Conventional. By comparing student and program profiles, PE fit indicates how well a student's interests match a study program. The article builds program environment profiles with the incumbent method, averaging the RIASEC scores of successful and persistent senior students, which the authors describe as "immune to rater bias, in contrast to profile generation based on expert ratings". The study applies this model through correlational fit and a derived program interest diversity measure (AD COR).
requirements: Person and environment must be represented on a commensurate scale so profiles can be compared, and interest must be a stable construct for incumbent-based environment profiles to be valid.
constraints: The article notes the magnitude of PE fit effects on study results remains debated, varying from very small to medium at best in prior literature.
target_learners: higher education students making study program choices
target_learning_goals: vocational interest assessment and study program orientation
examples: The study used the SIMON-I questionnaire to render student RIASEC profiles on 0–100 scales per dimension and averaged senior students' profiles to build program E-profiles.

article_title: The effects of vocational interest on study results: Student person - environment fit and program interest diversity.
citation: Schelfhout Stijn, Wille Bart, Fonteyne Lot, Roels Elisabeth, De Fruyt Filip, Duyck Wouter. (2019). The effects of vocational interest on study results: Student person – environment fit and program interest diversity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214618
title: Homogeneity theory of interest-based environment selection and program interest diversity
description: The article draws on "the age old homogeneity assumption" that people with similar vocational interests tend toward similar environments, so environments become inhabited by individuals with similar interest patterns. Applied to open-access higher education, it predicts students with high PE fit enroll in fitting programs, producing low program interest diversity, with residual diversity linked to controlled (external) motives of study choice. The article also proposes that high internal similarity makes student behavior more determined by the study environment than by individual interest patterns, motivating the comparison of program-level diversity effects against individual fit effects.
requirements: Measuring interest diversity requires a continuous, one-scale deviance measure that allows comparison across programs; the article derives AD COR by averaging rescaled correlational fit deviances (D COR) within programs.
constraints: The article warns against the ecological fallacy of assuming individual PE fit effects generalize to the program level, which is why it pits linear, negative, and curvilinear hypotheses against each other rather than assuming a direction.
target_learners: first-year students in open-access higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding how interest fit and interest diversity shape study results
examples: The study tested the homogeneity prediction by comparing interest diversity of 39 open-access programs with a restricted-access Medicine/Dentistry control group.

article_title: Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature.
citation: Mianda Solange, Voce Anna. (2018). Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3561-4
title: Content of clinical leadership development interventions should encompass a holistic conceptualization of clinical leadership
description: The review distinguishes interventions embracing a holistic conceptualization of clinical leadership — attending to clinical skills, leadership skills, team building, team management, the environment of care and service delivery — from selective, checklist-based interventions. It concludes intervention content "must encompass a holistic conceptualization of clinical leadership, with a focus on clinical skills and on competencies that support optimal clinical care". Holistic interventions can produce well trained and skilled clinical leaders.
requirements: Content spanning multiple dimensions of clinical leadership; longer training periods and greater expense may be needed
constraints: Holistic interventions may be expensive and require longer training periods; selective interventions may not be able to produce skilled clinical leaders
target_learners: novice and veteran frontline healthcare providers
target_learning_goals: clinical leadership competencies supporting quality and safe patient care
examples: Development of clinical skills was common to the majority of interventions; other content areas included personal development, teamwork, team management, service delivery, care processes and the environment of care

article_title: Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model.
citation: Williams, S. N., Thakore, B. K., & McGee, R. (2017). Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-01-0021
title: House's four-type social support typology as the analytical framework for coaching
description: The article adopts J. S. House's typology, in which "we take social support to encompass emotional support, informational support, appraisal support, and instrumental support." Emotional support involves empathy, trust, caring, and belonging; informational support is advice and guidance useful for problem solving; appraisal support is constructive feedback for self-assessment and validation of experience; instrumental support is tangible goods or services. The study applies the first three types as the coding framework for analyzing how coaches and peers supported URM PhD students, treating perceived social support—knowing support is available even if unused—as itself a determinant of effective coping.
requirements: Analysis of perceived social support requires asking whether individuals identify someone as a potential source of support, whether or not support is activated
constraints: The study focuses on perceived social support rather than objectively delivered support; instrumental support is defined but not analyzed in the reported results
target_learners: URM PhD students in biomedical sciences
target_learning_goals: Persistence toward academic science careers
Coping with graduate school stress and isolation
examples: The framework structured the qualitative coding of 96 interviews, with Table 2 reporting how many students were coded as receiving each support type from coaches versus peers
